Information Collection Strategies Experiment

Scaling consistency and case complexity

This deck covers two things: how consistent the scaling results are when the experiment is run several times, and how accuracy relates to how complex a case is, measured with the INTERMED score.

Research Question

What is the most accurate information collection strategy for a computer-based diagnostic system?

Every result in this deck serves this question: which way of collecting information about a patient leads a computer-based system to the right diagnosis most often.

Overview

The framework: an information collection strategy asks questions, one at a time. A simulated environment answers them: an LLM that reads the case study and searches the literature. After its question budget, the strategy gives a ranked list of diagnoses, which we score against the true diagnosis by ICD-11 code.

Scaling Consistency

Do the scaling results hold when rerun?

Part one. Earlier, each strategy and question budget was run once. A single run cannot tell a real difference from run-to-run noise, so we ran the scaling experiment again, several times.

Repeating the scaling experiment

Fresh runs at each question budget measure the spread.

4, 8, 16

iterations (scaling)

3

272

cases in each run, for all 4 strategies

In the next four plots, each line is the mean over the repetitions and the shaded band is ±1 standard deviation.

We reran the whole scaling experiment on the 272-case dataset, version 2: every strategy at 4, 8 and 16 questions, three times. The repetitions use the same configuration and differ only in the environment's seed (7, 8 and 9), so the variation comes from the models. At 16 questions the third repetition was still running when the plots were made, so those lines average two runs. Each plot shows top-k accuracy for k from 1 to 10: the share of cases whose true diagnosis is among the strategy's first k. The line is the mean of the runs and the band is one sample standard deviation either side.

Hypothesis-driven gains 10 points of top-10 accuracy from 4 to 8 questions, then only 4 more from 8 to 16. At top-1 it goes from 15.6% to 24.8% to 28.1%. The runs agree closely: the largest standard deviation is 2.9 points, at 8 questions.

Knowledge-driven

Knowledge-driven makes its largest gain between 8 and 16 questions (+10.6 points of top-10) and reaches the highest top-10 of any strategy, 55.5%. Its top-1 goes from 19.0% to 23.8% to 34.6%. It is also the most stable strategy: no standard deviation above 1.5 points. The two 16-question runs happened to score exactly the same top-10.

Channel-based gains about 10 points of top-10 from 4 to 8 questions and 7.5 more from 8 to 16, the largest total gain of the four (+17.6 points). Top-1 goes from 19.1% to 23.7% to 33.6%. Its widest spread is 2.7 points, at 8 questions.

Sequence-based is the best strategy at 4 questions (40.4% top-10, 22.7% top-1) but gains the least by 16 questions: +9.6 points of top-10, ending at 50.0%, behind knowledge-driven and channel-based. Top-1 goes from 22.7% to 28.7% to 33.3%. Its spread stays between 1.6 and 2.4 points.

Mean top-10 SD over the three budgets; the others 1.4 to 2.1.

Three insights from the four scaling slides, all on top-10 accuracy over the repetitions. Best scaling: knowledge-driven reaches the highest top-10 at 16 questions, 55.5%, ahead of channel-based (53.5%), sequence-based (50.0%) and hypothesis-driven (46.3%); it also has the highest top-1 there, 34.6%. Best at 4 questions: sequence-based, 40.4% top-10 and 22.7% top-1, the best of the four on both. Most consistent: knowledge-driven has the smallest run-to-run spread, a mean top-10 standard deviation of 0.9 points across the three budgets (1.1 over every k from 1 to 10); hypothesis-driven 1.4, channel-based 1.7 and sequence-based 2.1. The 16-question values average two runs.

Case complexity

Are complex cases harder to diagnose?

Part two. Accuracy is averaged over all 272 cases, but the cases are not equally hard. To look inside the average, we scored each case’s complexity and compared accuracy across complexity levels.

The INTERMED complexity score

Twenty items, each scored 0–3, add up to 0–60.

DomainHistoryCurrent statePrognosisVulnerabilitiesCare needs
BiologicalChronicityIllness severityComplicationsSelf-care limitsTherapeutic challenge
PsychologicalPsychiatric historyPsychiatric symptomsMental health threatCognitive, behaviouralMental health care
SocialChronic instabilityResidence, supportSocial vulnerabilitySocial integrationSocial support
Health carePrevious treatmentCurrent treatmentCare complexityPatient–providerCare coordination

Gemini 4 scored each case from its full text; 21 or more counts as high complexity.

INTERMED is a validated grid for biopsychosocial case complexity: four domains (biological, psychological, social, health care) by five categories, 20 items in all, each rated 0 (no need) to 3 (severe need). The total runs from 0 to 60, and 21 or more is the instrument’s cut-off for high complexity. We used the DDx experiment’s prompt word for word with Gemini 4 (seed 42, low reasoning), one call per case on the full case text; the run cost $2.96. Over the 272 cases the mean score is 19.3, the range 0 to 51, and 102 cases score 21 or more.

Top-1 accuracy by complexity

No steady decline; few cases score above 30.

Read with care

31–40 has 21 cases and 41–60 has 10, so one case moves a bar by 5 to 10 points.

Top-1 accuracy of each strategy at 8 questions (repetition 1), with the cases grouped into 10-point INTERMED buckets; 51–60 held one case and is folded into 41–60. The big middle bucket, 11–20 with 132 cases, is where most strategies score best, and sequence-based leads it at 35%. All strategies drop at 31–40. The jump at 41–60 rests on only ten cases (hypothesis-driven’s 50% is five of them), so it says little. At top-5 and top-10 the drop with complexity is clearer: about 50–57% at 11–20 against 33–43% above 20.

More questions help, and repeated runs agree

Every strategy gains 10 to 18 points of top-10 from 4 to 16 questions.

Runs agree: the top-10 spread is at most 2.9 points.

Top-1 shows no steady trend with complexity.

Three points to keep. One: more questions help every strategy, by 10 to 18 points of top-10 between 4 and 16 questions; knowledge-driven ends highest at 55.5%. Two: the results are consistent; across repetitions no strategy’s top-10 varies by more than 2.9 points (one standard deviation), smaller than most gaps between budgets. Three: at top-1 accuracy does not fall steadily with INTERMED complexity, though the most complex buckets hold few cases; at top-5 and top-10 complex cases do score lower.
